content: Idiopathic hypercalciuria is a hereditary metabolic condition characterized by an excessive excretion of calcium in the urine, despite normal calcium levels in the blood. This condition is associated with significant health issues, including kidney stone formation and bone demineralization. In children, idiopathic hypercalciuria can lead to recurrent blood in the urine (haematuria), urinary frequency and pain during urination (frequency-dysuria syndrome), urinary tract infections, and abdominal or lower back pain. Various pharmacological treatments have been proposed to reduce urinary calcium levels or decrease the likelihood of calcium crystallization in the urine. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness and potential adverse effects of pharmacological treatments in preventing complications and alleviating urological symptoms in patients with idiopathic hypercalciuria. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including MEDLINE, EMBASE, the Cochrane Renal Group's specialized register, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL). Additionally, relevant conference proceedings and reference lists of articles were manually reviewed. The inclusion criteria for the analysis were randomized controlled trials (RCTs) or quasi-RCTs that compared any pharmacological intervention for idiopathic hypercalciuria with placebo, other pharmacological treatments, or different dosages or administration methods of the same treatment. The studies had to have a minimum treatment duration of four months and a follow-up period of at least six months. Data extraction and study inclusion were performed by four authors, with disagreements resolved through discussion. The results were reported as risk ratios (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) or mean differences (MD). Five studies involving a total of 316 adult patients were included in the analysis. Four of these studies compared the use of thiazide diuretics with standard treatments, such as periodic clinical follow-ups, increased water intake, or specific dietary recommendations. One study examined the combined effect of thiazides and a neutral potassium salt. The findings demonstrated a significant reduction in the recurrence of kidney stones among patients treated with thiazides (RR 1.61, 95% CI 1.33 to 1.96), although the follow-up durations varied across studies. Additionally, the rate of stone formation was significantly lower in patients receiving diuretics (MD -0.18, 95% CI -0.30 to -0.06). The combination of thiazides and potassium salts was also found to significantly reduce urinary calcium excretion (calciuria) and vitamin D levels. The authors concluded that there is evidence supporting the use of thiazides in patients with idiopathic hypercalciuria and recurrent kidney stones. When combined with a normal or modified diet, thiazides administered over periods ranging from five months to three years were effective in reducing the recurrence of kidney stones and the rate of stone formation. Furthermore, the combination of thiazides and neutral potassium phosphate was shown to decrease urinary calcium levels in symptomatic patients. However, no studies were identified that evaluated the effects of pharmacological treatments on other clinical complications or on asymptomatic idiopathic hypercalciuria.
